title: A Sagging Ridge on the House
description: A dip in the roof ridge can be a tired deck or a rafter problem. One is roofing work. The other needs a framer before any new shingle goes down.
html:
Stand across the street and look along the ridge. A straight ridge looks like a line. A sag looks like the house exhaled. People notice it when they are thinking about new shingles, which is the right time to notice it and the wrong time to hide it under a new roof.

Deck waves and a true sag are different

Waves between the rafters, a quilted look in the shingles, usually mean the deck is thin or the supports are far apart. That can be repaired when the roof is off, with thicker sheathing or blocking. A dip in the ridge itself, running along the beam line, is the frame: rafters, a ridge board, collar ties, or a wall under the middle of the house that has settled. New shingles will follow that dip. They will not lift it.

We do not shingle over a structure that is still moving. If the ridge is the problem, a framer looks at it before we price a roof. Sometimes the fix is reinforcement in the attic and the roof can follow. Sometimes an engineer needs to say what the house is doing. Our job is to recognize which one we are looking at, not to sell a laminate that disguises it for one listing photo.

Old houses are allowed to be old

Not every slight bow is a failure. Houses settle. A ridge that has looked like that for twenty years, with no new cracks in the drywall and no doors suddenly sticking, is not an emergency. A ridge that dropped after a storm, or a leak that rotted the joint where the rafters meet, is. The attic tells on it: cracked wood, nails pulled, daylight at a joint that used to be tight.

If you can see the dip from the curb, ask for a roof inspection that includes the attic, not only the shingles. We will tell you whether to call a framer first. Request a free inspection or call (281) 541-0027.
